meta.title: Chiesi Data Bootcamp — Agility → Business Questions → Shared Exploration → Data Skills → Hackathon Builds → Decision Use → Cases
meta.subtitle: A simple knowledge lattice for professional learners using Excel, Python, data cleaning, prompts and hackathon practice to move from business challenge to useful action.
meta.domainName: Data bootcamp learning journey for Chiesi professional learners
meta.searchPlaceholder: agility, hackathon, Excel, Python, pandas, data cleaning, pivot tables, joins, data dictionary, prompts, Similar Deals, Green Analysis, Pipeline Next, interprofessional learning, decision pack…
meta.userContextPlaceholder: e.g., Similar Deals team; Green Analysis data slice; Pipeline Next review pack; beginner Python confidence; Excel skills; hackathon role; cross-functional challenge…
meta.promptTemplate:
You are helping a Chiesi Data Bootcamp team develop agility in the face of linked business and technical challenges.

User context (if provided):
{{USER_CONTEXT}}

Selected concepts:
{{SELECTED_TITLES}}

Details:
{{SELECTED_DETAILS}}

Trace paths:
{{TRACE_SUMMARY}}

Write a practical learning narrative showing how the team grows more agile. Keep the language clear and concrete. Show how the team moves from a business question to a small data slice, then to cleaning, Excel or Python work, a prompt or prototype, expert feedback, and a clearer next action.

Include:
- the business challenge and the decision it should improve
- the people involved and what each profession or role contributes
- the data needed, including messy fields, missing values, IDs, units and dates
- the simple technical skills used or noticed: Excel tables, formulas, pivots, Python, pandas, charts, prompts, joins, checks
- what happens in the hackathon: problem exploration, safe experiments, build, test, demo and feedback
- how the team handles uncertainty, judgement and caveats
- how the work increases agility: more options, better questions, faster learning, clearer action
- one next step after the hackathon

levels.title: Agility and shared purpose
levels.hint: Broad aim: help people see more options, act with data, and join business and technical work.

levels.title: Business questions and value
levels.hint: Start with the decision, the user, the friction, and the value to the business.

levels.title: Shared problem exploration
levels.hint: Hackathon teams, students, sponsors and experts explore the problem space together before choosing tools.

levels.title: Data and tool basics
levels.hint: Awareness of Excel, Python, data cleaning, joins, files, charts, prompts and simple models.

levels.title: Hackathon build moves
levels.hint: Practical moves used during the bootcamp: define, clean, code, prompt, build, test, explain and demo.

levels.title: Outputs, use and testing
levels.hint: Decision packs, simple dashboards, checks, caveats, workflow fit, adoption and next steps.

levels.title: Cases, examples and watch-outs
levels.hint: Specific Chiesi case instances and common risks such as dirty data, false precision and tool-first thinking.

nodes.label: Agility to act
nodes.summary: The ability to move from unclear need to useful action with data and technology.
nodes.bodyHtml: Agility means moving between business meaning and technical detail: frame, explore, clean, build, test, explain and act.

nodes.label: Technology opens options
nodes.summary: Technical awareness changes what people think is possible.
nodes.bodyHtml: When learners see what Excel, Python, prompts and simple models can do, they start to imagine new ways to organise work.

nodes.label: Data as a shared asset
nodes.summary: Data becomes more useful when departments treat it as a shared resource.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp shifts data from a local file owned by one team to a shared object that helps many teams make better decisions.

nodes.label: Whole-business view
nodes.summary: Better data work helps teams see links across strategy, sustainability, pipeline, finance and operations.
nodes.bodyHtml: The aim is not a single tool. It is a more joined-up view of how decisions, evidence and people connect across Chiesi.

nodes.label: Human judgement with tools
nodes.summary: Tools should support judgement rather than replace it.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp teaches where automation can help, where it should only assist, and where expert judgement must remain in charge.

nodes.label: Confidence with caveats
nodes.summary: Act with more confidence while being clear about limits and uncertainty.
nodes.bodyHtml: Good data work does not pretend to know everything. It makes assumptions, gaps and caveats visible so action can be safer.

nodes.label: Decision-backwards thinking
nodes.summary: Start from the decision or meeting that should improve.
nodes.bodyHtml: Instead of asking which tool to use, teams ask which decision should be easier, faster or more trusted after the prototype exists.

nodes.label: Real business need
nodes.summary: Anchor the work in live organisational friction rather than abstract data practice.
nodes.bodyHtml: The three cases matter because they are real Chiesi problems: deal comparison, Net Zero analysis and pipeline review.

nodes.label: Problem space first
nodes.summary: Explore the problem before choosing the solution.
nodes.bodyHtml: A hackathon is stronger when the team first maps decisions, users, data, risks and success signals.

nodes.label: Decision audience
nodes.summary: Know who will use the output and what they need from it.
nodes.bodyHtml: A sponsor, asset lead, sustainability team or executive board may need different detail, caveats and formats.

nodes.label: Business friction
nodes.summary: Name where time, trust or coordination is lost.
nodes.bodyHtml: Friction may sit in search, data cleaning, agreeing definitions, reconciling versions, writing packs or checking assumptions.

nodes.label: Data-to-action chain
nodes.summary: Show how data becomes evidence, evidence becomes a decision, and a decision becomes action.
nodes.bodyHtml: This chain stops the work becoming a dashboard with no clear use.

nodes.label: Small slice, big learning
nodes.summary: Use a small data slice to prove the idea before scaling.
nodes.bodyHtml: A few assets, a few deals or a few emissions categories can teach more than an over-large dataset that cannot be handled in time.

nodes.label: Inside and outside data
nodes.summary: Combine internal data with useful external evidence where needed.
nodes.bodyHtml: Similar Deals may need public deal announcements; Green Analysis may need emission factors; Pipeline Next may need internal metrics and narratives.

nodes.label: Business story
nodes.summary: Turn numbers, text and caveats into a story that supports discussion.
nodes.bodyHtml: A useful output explains what changed, what matters, what is uncertain and what should happen next.

nodes.label: Synergy goal
nodes.summary: Use the bootcamp to improve links between teams, data and decisions.
nodes.bodyHtml: The deeper value is better coordination: people understand each other's data, limits, priorities and needs.

nodes.label: Interprofessional working
nodes.summary: People from different roles learn with, from and about each other.
nodes.bodyHtml: Business, technical, scientific, finance, sustainability and governance roles each see a different part of the problem.

nodes.label: Students as problem explorers
nodes.summary: Students and learners help explore the space, not just execute tasks.
nodes.bodyHtml: In the hackathon, students can ask fresh questions, map options, test small ideas and make hidden assumptions visible.

nodes.label: Shared language
nodes.summary: Build simple words for data, business needs and technical moves.
nodes.bodyHtml: Words like field, key, join, flag, caveat, scenario and decision pack help teams work together.

nodes.label: Shared work objects
nodes.summary: Use maps, tables, cards and prototypes as things people can discuss together.
nodes.bodyHtml: A data dictionary, prototype screen or one-page pack helps different professions point at the same thing while bringing different expertise.

nodes.label: Sponsor-team-student triangle
nodes.summary: Link sponsor need, team knowledge and student experimentation.
nodes.bodyHtml: Sponsors clarify value; professional teams provide context; students help prototype, question and show possibilities.

nodes.label: Safe to try
nodes.summary: Use the hackathon as a safe place for experiments.
nodes.bodyHtml: Small trials reduce fear: a failed join, prompt or chart becomes useful learning rather than a project failure.

nodes.label: Fast feedback
nodes.summary: Build quickly and learn from reactions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Short loops between prototype and expert response help teams discover what matters.

nodes.label: Role switching
nodes.summary: Let business people try technical questions and technical people ask business questions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Agility grows when people cross role boundaries enough to understand each other's constraints.

nodes.label: Judgement mapping
nodes.summary: Mark which decisions are human-owned and which can be supported by tools.
nodes.bodyHtml: Teams map what should be automated, assisted or left to expert review.

nodes.label: Assumptions out loud
nodes.summary: Make hidden assumptions visible early.
nodes.bodyHtml: Assumptions about similarity, emissions drivers, KPI definitions or data quality should be spoken and recorded.

nodes.label: Peer teaching
nodes.summary: Participants teach each other small skills at the moment of need.
nodes.bodyHtml: One person may know Excel pivots, another may know Python, another may know the business rule. The hackathon lets these skills circulate.

nodes.label: User story
nodes.summary: State what a user needs in plain language.
nodes.bodyHtml: For example: as a portfolio reviewer, I need mismatches flagged before the meeting so the discussion can focus on decisions.

nodes.label: Data owner conversation
nodes.summary: Talk to the people who know where the data comes from and what it means.
nodes.bodyHtml: Data owners explain fields, gaps, update rhythms, definitions and safe use limits.

nodes.label: Check the question
nodes.summary: Step back and ask whether the team is solving the right problem.
nodes.bodyHtml: This is the simple form of double-loop learning: not just doing the task better, but questioning the task itself.

nodes.label: Excel tables
nodes.summary: Use structured tables rather than loose spreadsheet ranges.
nodes.bodyHtml: Tables make sorting, filtering, formulas and later import into Python or Power BI easier.

nodes.label: Spreadsheet formulas
nodes.summary: Use basic formulas to compute fields, check values and create quick prototypes.
nodes.bodyHtml: Awareness of IF, XLOOKUP, COUNTIF and simple date calculations helps learners see how rules become logic.

nodes.label: Pivot tables and charts
nodes.summary: Summarise data quickly by category, time, owner or status.
nodes.bodyHtml: Pivots help participants explore patterns before writing code.

nodes.label: Power Query awareness
nodes.summary: Know that repeat cleaning steps can be recorded and refreshed.
nodes.bodyHtml: Power Query can make Excel cleaning more repeatable without requiring full coding confidence.

nodes.label: Data dictionary
nodes.summary: Define fields, units, owners, sources and meanings.
nodes.bodyHtml: A data dictionary turns messy files into shared knowledge and reduces argument about definitions.

nodes.label: CSV and JSON files
nodes.summary: Understand common file formats used in data work and prototypes.
nodes.bodyHtml: CSV holds tables; JSON can hold structured records, app settings or concept lattices.

nodes.label: Data cleaning
nodes.summary: Fix messy names, formats, blanks, duplicates and inconsistent categories.
nodes.bodyHtml: Cleaning is not low-level admin. It is where teams learn what the organisation really knows and does not know.

nodes.label: Missing data
nodes.summary: Notice blanks, unknowns and fields that cannot be trusted.
nodes.bodyHtml: A missing value may be harmless, or it may block a decision. The team must know the difference.

nodes.label: Data joining
nodes.summary: Combine tables using a shared key.
nodes.bodyHtml: Joining deal records, emissions factors or asset metrics is often the step that creates new insight.

nodes.label: IDs and keys
nodes.summary: Use stable identifiers to link records safely.
nodes.bodyHtml: Asset IDs, deal IDs, supplier IDs or category codes prevent accidental mismatches.

nodes.label: Dates and time fields
nodes.summary: Treat dates as data, not text.
nodes.bodyHtml: Milestones, review dates, announcement dates and emissions periods all need consistent formats.

nodes.label: Units and categories
nodes.summary: Keep units, categories and labels consistent.
nodes.bodyHtml: Emissions factors, currencies, stages and scopes become misleading if units or labels drift.

nodes.label: Python basics
nodes.summary: Know enough Python to read, transform and check data.
nodes.bodyHtml: Awareness of variables, lists, functions and loops helps learners understand what code can automate.

nodes.label: Pandas data frames
nodes.summary: Use Python tables for filtering, grouping, joining and cleaning.
nodes.bodyHtml: Pandas is a practical bridge from Excel awareness to reproducible data workflows.

nodes.label: Notebooks
nodes.summary: Use notebooks to mix code, notes, charts and explanation.
nodes.bodyHtml: A notebook can become a shared learning record for the hackathon team.

nodes.label: Simple statistics
nodes.summary: Use counts, averages, ranges, rates and simple comparisons.
nodes.bodyHtml: Many useful prototypes need clear simple statistics before any advanced model.

nodes.label: Charts and visuals
nodes.summary: Make patterns visible with simple plots.
nodes.bodyHtml: A good chart can show a trend, a gap, an outlier or a mismatch quickly.

nodes.label: Prompt basics
nodes.summary: Ask AI tools clear, bounded questions and require evidence or caveats.
nodes.bodyHtml: Prompts can help summarise, structure fields, generate code or draft narratives, but outputs need checking.

nodes.label: API awareness
nodes.summary: Know that tools can exchange data through interfaces.
nodes.bodyHtml: Learners do not need to build every API, but awareness helps them imagine more connected workflows.

nodes.label: Database and SQL awareness
nodes.summary: Know that larger data often lives in databases and can be queried.
nodes.bodyHtml: Basic awareness of tables, queries and filters helps learners talk to data and IT teams.

nodes.label: Reproducible files
nodes.summary: Keep clear versions of data, code, prompts and outputs.
nodes.bodyHtml: A prototype is more useful if another person can rerun it and understand what changed.

nodes.label: Challenge definition
nodes.summary: Write the challenge in a few clear sentences.
nodes.bodyHtml: A short definition helps the team agree what the prototype is for and what it must not do.

nodes.label: Data inventory
nodes.summary: List sources, owners, fields, quality issues and readiness.
nodes.bodyHtml: The inventory turns vague data talk into a practical checklist.

nodes.label: Sample dataset
nodes.summary: Prepare a small safe dataset for building and testing.
nodes.bodyHtml: A simulated or cleaned slice lets students work without exposing sensitive values.

nodes.label: Prototype backlog
nodes.summary: Turn needs into small build tasks.
nodes.bodyHtml: Tasks may include clean date fields, join tables, create a chart, write a flag rule or test a prompt.

nodes.label: Prototype plan
nodes.summary: Decide what can be shown by the end of the hackathon.
nodes.bodyHtml: The plan keeps ambition realistic while still showing a path to value.

nodes.label: Code walkthrough
nodes.summary: Explain what the code does in plain language.
nodes.bodyHtml: Walkthroughs help non-coders see the logic and help coders catch wrong assumptions.

nodes.label: Pair work
nodes.summary: Pair people with different strengths to build and check together.
nodes.bodyHtml: A business expert and a student coder can move faster together than either can alone.

nodes.label: Rapid build
nodes.summary: Build a rough version quickly so the team can react.
nodes.bodyHtml: A rough working thing often teaches more than a perfect plan.

nodes.label: Prompt-to-code support
nodes.summary: Use prompts to help draft code, formulas or data steps, then test them.
nodes.bodyHtml: AI can speed up learning when it is treated as a helper that must show its logic and be checked.

nodes.label: Human-in-loop rules
nodes.summary: Write rules for when a person must review the output.
nodes.bodyHtml: This prevents a prototype from pretending to make decisions it cannot safely make.

nodes.label: Flag rules
nodes.summary: Create simple checks for missing, stale, conflicting or out-of-range data.
nodes.bodyHtml: Flags help the team see where attention is needed before a meeting or decision.

nodes.label: Scenario model
nodes.summary: Compare possible futures under clear assumptions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Scenario work helps Green Analysis move from history to action.

nodes.label: Similarity score
nodes.summary: Rank candidates using visible criteria.
nodes.bodyHtml: A useful score explains why something is close and where the match is weak.

nodes.label: Decision pack builder
nodes.summary: Create a short output that supports a meeting.
nodes.bodyHtml: The pack should show evidence, caveats, flags and next actions.

nodes.label: Expert validation
nodes.summary: Ask experts whether the output makes sense and where it fails.
nodes.bodyHtml: Expert feedback turns a demo into a learning loop.

nodes.label: Demo story
nodes.summary: Tell the story of the prototype clearly.
nodes.bodyHtml: A good demo shows the business question, the data, the method, the caveat and the next step.

nodes.label: Version control awareness
nodes.summary: Know why teams track changes in code and data.
nodes.bodyHtml: Even if learners do not master Git, they should understand why versions matter.

nodes.label: Decision pack
nodes.summary: A short, trusted pack that helps a real meeting or choice.
nodes.bodyHtml: The pack brings together key numbers, narrative, caveats and suggested next actions.

nodes.label: Explainable output
nodes.summary: The result says why it reached a ranking, flag or scenario.
nodes.bodyHtml: People can challenge an explainable output rather than accept or reject a black box.

nodes.label: Uncertainty display
nodes.summary: Show what is unknown, estimated, weak or disputed.
nodes.bodyHtml: Uncertainty is not a defect. It guides where to check, learn or act carefully.

nodes.label: Quality checks
nodes.summary: Checks for missing data, duplicates, stale fields and inconsistent units.
nodes.bodyHtml: Simple checks can prevent poor data being turned into polished but wrong outputs.

nodes.label: Simple dashboard
nodes.summary: A focused screen for exploring a small number of useful measures.
nodes.bodyHtml: The best dashboard answers a decision need rather than showing every available metric.

nodes.label: Assist, do not replace
nodes.summary: Use tools to prepare, highlight and explain; keep responsibility clear.
nodes.bodyHtml: The prototype should help people see and act, not hide judgement inside a machine.

nodes.label: Workflow fit
nodes.summary: The output fits the meeting, template, cadence and tool environment.
nodes.bodyHtml: A technically clever prototype will fail if it does not fit how people actually work.

nodes.label: Adoption route
nodes.summary: Describe how the prototype could become part of normal work.
nodes.bodyHtml: This includes ownership, support, governance, training, data refresh and next development steps.

nodes.label: Evidence and caveats
nodes.summary: State what the evidence supports and what it does not support.
nodes.bodyHtml: Caveats protect the team from overclaiming and help decision-makers use the result wisely.

nodes.label: Success measures
nodes.summary: Define how the team will know the work helped.
nodes.bodyHtml: Measures may include time saved, fewer version conflicts, better comparator quality or clearer scenario choices.

nodes.label: Reusable workflow
nodes.summary: A process that can be repeated on another case or dataset.
nodes.bodyHtml: Reusability is a sign that the team has built capability, not just a one-off demo.

nodes.label: Next steps after the hackathon
nodes.summary: Convert the demo into a learning plan and delivery path.
nodes.bodyHtml: The next step may be better data, user testing, governance review, a second data slice or a stronger prototype.

nodes.label: Light data governance
nodes.summary: Use simple ownership, access and quality rules from the start.
nodes.bodyHtml: Even early prototypes need clarity about safe data, owners, field meanings and limits.

nodes.label: Measured improvement
nodes.summary: Show how the prototype improves time, trust, clarity or coordination.
nodes.bodyHtml: Improvement should be visible enough that sponsors can decide whether to invest further.

nodes.label: Similar Deals case
nodes.summary: Find a useful pool of comparable inorganic growth deals.
nodes.bodyHtml: The team must define what similar means for a decision, not just search for matching keywords.

nodes.label: False friend comparator
nodes.summary: Two deals look similar on the surface but differ in business logic.
nodes.bodyHtml: A therapy-area match may hide differences in stage, modality, deal type, financial terms or strategic rationale.

nodes.label: Minimum deal record
nodes.summary: Deal ID, date, parties, deal type, asset features, financial terms and confidence notes.
nodes.bodyHtml: This is the practical table structure needed before ranking can be trusted.

nodes.label: Green Analysis case
nodes.summary: Turn emissions history into forecasts, scenarios and decision evidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: The team links emissions, activity, drivers, interventions and uncertainty.

nodes.label: Factor revision mistake
nodes.summary: A change in emission factors looks like real operational progress.
nodes.bodyHtml: The model must separate accounting change from real change in business activity.

nodes.label: Supplier priority example
nodes.summary: Compare emissions size, confidence and ability to influence suppliers.
nodes.bodyHtml: The best action may be to improve data first, not simply chase the biggest number.

nodes.label: Pipeline Next case
nodes.summary: Create a reproducible review pack from metrics and narratives.
nodes.bodyHtml: The team combines asset data, KPIs, narrative extracts, flags and summary text.

nodes.label: Conflicting asset status
nodes.summary: One source says on track, another says delayed, another lists a risk.
nodes.bodyHtml: The prototype should surface the mismatch before the meeting.

nodes.label: Integrated asset row
nodes.summary: One row per asset per review with key fields, KPIs, flags and notes.
nodes.bodyHtml: This simple structure helps teams see what must be joined and checked.

nodes.label: Tool-first thinking
nodes.summary: The team starts with AI or dashboards before defining the business need.
nodes.bodyHtml: This often creates impressive outputs that do not help the real decision.

nodes.label: AI smooths conflict
nodes.summary: A summary sounds fluent but hides data conflict.
nodes.bodyHtml: The tool must show mismatches and caveats, not write around them.

nodes.label: False precision
nodes.summary: Charts or forecasts look exact even when the inputs are weak.
nodes.bodyHtml: The team should show ranges, assumptions and confidence rather than overclaim.

nodes.label: Dirty data blocks progress
nodes.summary: Messy formats, blanks, duplicates and weak IDs slow the hackathon.
nodes.bodyHtml: This is why data cleaning and data dictionaries are core skills, not side tasks.

nodes.label: Return to silos
nodes.summary: After the hackathon, teams go back to separate files and local habits.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp should leave shared artefacts, owners and next steps so learning continues.

nodes.label: Over-automation
nodes.summary: The prototype makes a judgement that should remain with experts.
nodes.bodyHtml: Human-in-loop rules protect trust and safe use.

nodes.label: Excel first clean
nodes.summary: Use Excel tables, filters and pivots to inspect the data before coding.
nodes.bodyHtml: This gives all participants a way into the data, even if they are new to Python.

nodes.label: Python join demo
nodes.summary: Use pandas to join two tables and flag mismatches.
nodes.bodyHtml: A short demo can show how repeated manual work might become reproducible.

nodes.label: Student demo pitch
nodes.summary: Students present what they built, what failed and what should happen next.
nodes.bodyHtml: The pitch is a learning moment: it makes technical possibility visible to business sponsors.

nodes.label: Hackathon day one
nodes.summary: Teams map the problem, inspect data and choose a small build target.
nodes.bodyHtml: The first day should protect time for exploration before rushing into code.

nodes.label: Show-and-tell loop
nodes.summary: A short demo is shown to experts, then improved from feedback.
nodes.bodyHtml: This loop turns the hackathon from a coding sprint into a business learning process.
